newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - June 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - June 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- MANUFACTURING OUTPUT UP

The results of the latest survey from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply suggests that manufacturing output is rising faster then at any time for the past two years, with companies cashing in on the strength of domestic demand to offset weakness in overseas sales caused by the strong pound. The results are expected to allay fears of a one-sided recovery in which manufacturing trails the service sector.
-- TRADEPOINT CALLS FOR ONE MILLION STG

London's rival stock market, Tradepoint, is seeking to raise one million stg from its shareholders to allow it to keep trading after failing to obtain long-term finance by a weekend deadline. The company faced administration if Williams de Broe, the stockbroker, had not agreed to provide the interim finance. Michael Waller-Bridge, chief executive, admitted that there had been a "last minute glitch" in receiving subscriptions from new investors.
-- BA GROUND STAFF TO VOTE ON STRIKE

A dispute involving the contracting out of catering services could lead to a strike by 9,000 ground staff at British Airways. The strike could hit the airline at the height of the summer season. This follows the announcement by the Transport and General Workers' Union that it is to hold a ballot with results to be declared on June 30. Robert Ayling, BA's chief executive, warned union members of extensive contingency plans if they voted in favour of action.
THE TIMES
-- CITY RELIEF AT NEW BANK ADVISERS

The City has expressed relief over Chancellor Gordon Brown's announcement of the four external advisers to the Bank of England's new Monetary Policy Committee. The appointees are Dr DeAnne Julius, chief economist at British Airways, Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser at the Treasury, and Professor Charles Goodhart and Professor Willem Buiter, two academics. Economists said the new members added creditability to the committee which has responsibility for fixing interest rate policy.
-- FRENCH SOCIALISTS' WIN UPSETS MARKETS

Markets across Europe are in chaos after the Socialist victory in the French elections as analysts try to assess the consequences for economic and monetary union. Trading on the Paris bourse was volatile as foreign investors pulled out of the market at first. The German mark emerged as the big loser as traders interpreted the Socialist victory in France as evidence that there will be a broad but soft euro.
-- DEBUT DROP FOR HALIFAX AS MEMBERS TAKE WINDFALL

The first day of trading for Halifax shares saw them fall by more than five per cent as more than two million savers and borrowers in the converting building society pulled out, making an average of 2,200 stg. Halifax was given a market value of 18 billion stg, slightly more than Barclays. Shares in the banking sector fell with some commentators suggesting that institutional investors were selling shares short to deflate the sector's high rating.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BUDGET DAY BREAK WITH TRADITION

Chancellor Gordon Brown has announced that Budget day will be Wednesday July 2. This signals a break from the tradition of delivering Budgets on a Tuesday. The Budget is expected to introduce tighter fiscal policy to take some of the heat out of the economy. City economists say that survey evidence of the strength of manufacturing output increases the likelihood that the Bank will increase rates before the Budget.
-- SAVING FOR GAS METER PAYERS

Midlands Gas is set to introduce a radical departure for the industry's competition strategy by offering a 30 stg discount to low income customers. This will put Midland ahead of rivals in cutting the cost of gas to pre-payment meter consumers. Gas supply companies are preparing to compete with the former British Gas GAS.L to supply up to 18 million domestic customers when competition goes national next year.
-- CHRISTIE'S SUBPOENA IN U.S. ANTI-TRUST CASE

Christie's International plc has received a grand jury subpoena for documents as part of a Justice Department anti-trust investigation in the U.S. art market. The company denies any wrongdoing and is co-operating with the investigations saying it understands that other U.S. auctioneers and several prominent New York art dealers have also been required to provide information.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- LANICA TO STAY SUSPENDED

The investment vehicle set up by Andrew Regan, Lanica Trust, published its long-delayed results despite failing to resolve the problems with the Stock Exchange which have prevented the group's shares being relisted. The group said the suspension would be continued until there was a resolution to the private prosecution brought against Regan and his associates after the alleged theft of confidential documents and a Serious Fraud Office investigation.
-- METROLINE CHIEFS SET FOR WINDFALL ON FLOTATION

Directors of Metroline, one of the last independent bus companies of the old London Transport network, will receive millions of pounds stg when the operator is floated on the stock market in the summer. The group is looking to raise up to five million stg through an institutional placing, which would value the company at 35 million stg. Staff will also share the payout,
with windfalls of up to 27,000 stg.
-- HODGSON RESIGNS FROM RONSON

Howard Hodgson has resigned as chief executive of Ronson, the lighters group, after it warned it would see a two million stg loss for last year, double the amount the group predicted three months ago. Non-executive director, Alan Kilkenny, said there had been no pressure for the resignation from the rest of the board at Ronson. Hodgson will be replaced on an interim basis by David Clipsham.
